lesson.title: The Router's Quick Look: Where Processing Delay Comes From
lesson.summary: Processing delay is the small amount of time a router spends checking and routing a packet before queuing it for transmission, usually the smallest of the four delay components on modern hardware.
lesson.body:
Processing delay is the time a router or switch spends examining a packet after it fully arrives and before that packet is placed into the outgoing queue for transmission. During this time the device is not moving any bits toward the destination. It is deciding what to do with the packet it already has in hand.

That decision involves several small steps. The router reads the packet header, checks it for bit errors using a checksum, looks up the destination address in its routing or forwarding table to determine which outgoing interface to use, and often decrements a field like the IP time to live counter. Only after all of that finishes does the packet move into the appropriate output queue, where queuing delay, covered in the previous chapter, takes over.

In modern routers this step is fast. A hardware based router built around dedicated forwarding chips can complete a lookup and header check in a few microseconds. Suppose a path from your laptop to a server crosses 10 routers, each contributing 5 microseconds of processing delay. The total processing delay across the whole path is 10 times 5 microseconds, or 50 microseconds. Compare that to the propagation delay of sending a signal across a continent, roughly 20 to 30 milliseconds depending on distance and medium. Fifty microseconds is thousands of times smaller, which is why processing delay is usually the least significant term in a latency budget on modern hardware.

This was not always true. Older routers that made forwarding decisions in general purpose software, rather than dedicated hardware, could take much longer per packet and were far more sensitive to how busy the device's processor was at that moment. Even on modern equipment, processing delay can grow noticeably when a device does more than basic forwarding, such as deep packet inspection, firewall rule matching, or encryption and decryption, since each of those adds real computation before the packet can move on.

Processing delay typically comes first in the sequence at each router: a packet is received, processed, queued, and then transmitted onto the next link, where it experiences propagation delay before arriving at the next device and starting the cycle again. Network engineers refer to processing delay, queuing delay, transmission delay, and propagation delay together as the four components of nodal delay, the total delay contributed by a single hop.

Summing nodal delay across every router on a path is what produces the end to end latency a packet actually experiences, tying this chapter back to the broader concept of latency. Because processing delay is usually small and fairly stable on modern networks, most of the variation you observe in real world latency measurements comes from queuing delay instead, which is exactly why network troubleshooting tends to focus on congestion rather than router processing speed.
